newsitem.title: CONGO: Five Western armies, barely in step, on Zaire watch.
newsitem.headline: Five Western armies, barely in step, on Zaire watch.

text.p: Military forces from five Western armies, in a state of permanent and costly alert in Congo, now probably outnumber the foreigners in Zaire's capital they came to evacuate.
Paradoxes surround an operation that began nearly two months ago and whose narrowly defined mission belies the political divisions between theoretical allies.

The United States, Belgium, Britain, France and Portugal - the order corresponds with their strength on the ground - now have well over 4,000 soldiers, aviators and sailors mustered in Congo's capital Brazzaville, its oil city of Pointe Noire and on a U.S. amphibious assault ship off the coast.

A dash of military legend is provided by the arrival this week of a company of the Foreign Legion, France's spearhead whenever Africa boils over, and the presence of 50 Gurkhas, Britain's Nepalese warriors.
Curiously, two of the countries involved, the United States and Britain, claim to have zero interests to defend in Zaire, Africa's third largest state where rebels are poised to take power.

American and British citizens still in Kinshasa number a few hundred, diehards who have ignored repeated advice to leave and perhaps absolved their governments of blame if they lose their lives or property.

Bristling with state-of-the-art weaponry and training every day with helicopters, hovercraft and speedboats, the Western contingents represent a daunting deterrent to any Zairean adversary planning to assault the dwindling group of foreigners across the mighty Zaire river in Kinshasa.
Yet spokesmen for all the armies in Brazzaville, who have each picked different names for the operation, insist their sole mission is evacuation when ordered by their governments.
"We are not interested in the internal politics of Zaire or taking any faction's side," said Commander Bob Anderson, spokesman for the American operation, code-named "Guardian Retrieval".

However often this assertion is repeated, it will not be believed by the collapsing regime of President Mobutu Sese Seko. After 32 years in power, Mobutu's writ is now limited to a rapidly shrinking enclave of territory and his supporters accuse the U.S. and Britain of sponsoring rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
The same suspicion is harboured by the French government, diplomats in central Africa concur, and French officers in Brazzaville are wryly quizzical about the real agenda of Washington and London.
The five armies in Congo have no joint command and control structure.
Asked why, Commander Anderson referred reporters to the State Department and replied: "That really is not a question we have to deal with here."
The contingents have liaison officers to ensure each knows the other's plans in case of an evacuation.
"There is no real coordination but everyone knows where the other is or will be. It is more like cooperation," said Captain Alexis Jaraud, spokesman for the French army's Operation Pelican.
The differences affect more mundane matters. American troops eat their powder rations while Belgian and French army caterers buy fresh produce and cook succulent meals between dress rehearsals.

Captain Jaraud lives with the 300-strong French contingent in tents or a bombed-out office block. "That is our tradition in Africa. Operationally we didn't want all our people around the swimming pool."
The U.S. and British troops have opted for hotel life, albeit stacked into rooms in fours and fives.

British officers quickly inform reporters that the formula - - a private sector approach to military deployment -- is actually cheaper than flying out the logistical paraphernalia required by armies in the rough.
